summary:
UMBRA is a free web app that aims at planning future landing sites in an easier and more interactive way. It allows you to see any spot on the Moon and any date, when the Sun is up and when Earth is in view for radio contact. Those two things decide when a lander can work and they change every time a launch slips.

Pick a past mission site or drop a pin anywhere. The app shows the Sun's elevation, the time left until sunset and Earthset and the sunlight and Earth-view windows over the next 60 days. You can compare three sites side by side, stand on the surface to see the real horizon and play time forward. Keep a planned landing date as a baseline, move the date and see at once what a delay gains or loses.

Two modes in the app allow the everyday person and someone who wants to plan an actual mission to use it in the way they would want to. One allows the person to just have fun and learn in the process and the other gives suggestions with detailed reasons on why their lander should land there

It runs on NASA data: LOLA terrain for the horizon at each site, and the JPL DE440 ephemeris for Sun and Earth positions, including libration. Our measurements match closely to ones calculated my other in the field like JPL.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that answers one planning question: at this spot on the Moon, on this date, is there sunlight for power and a clear line to Earth for radio? The app shows data like the Sun's elevation, the time left until sunset and Earthset, and every sunlight and Earth-view window over the next 60 days. You can compare three sites side by side and pick what will be the best for your lander and mission considerations. Look back at past, present and future missions and see what they plan to do and what the landing conditions are

How it works

For each site the app builds a terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation data, using 720 directions around the site. It takes Sun and Earth positions from the NASA JPL DE440 ephemeris, including libration, and tests them against that horizon. The Sun and Earth are treated as discs, not points, there is no refraction because the Moon has no atmosphere, and eclipses are included.

Benefits and intended impact

Delays or unforeseen circumstances can bring about delays, causing the landing days to slip. Such delays change the lighting and the radio link with earth and these need to he acounted for. A planner can keep the planned date as a baseline, move the date, and see at once what the delay gains or loses. Site rankings, shareable links and CSV export support early trade studies. Explorer mode gives students and the public the same accurate picture without the jargon.

Validity

Our angles match JPL Horizons to within 0.001°. Our sunlight shares match NASA GSFC's illumination map (r = 0.988), and we reproduce published figures for well-lit polar ridges. The method and its limits are documented in the repository.

Tools

TypeScript, React and Vite, with three.js for the 3D Moon. Python and NASA's SPICE toolkit prepared the terrain and ephemeris data. It is a static site on GitHub Pages, so it needs no server or account, and the code is open source under Apache 2.0.

How it is creative

It joins a mission planner's tool and a public explainer in one app with two modes. With the 3d model of the moon, it is easy to visualise whatever you want to do. You can go from orbit to standing beside a lander and watch the Sun graze the real horizon. or you can easily compare where such landing sites are and decide where you craft should land

What we considered

Accuracy before appearance. We wanted to ensure that regardless of who you are, that you get the right info. We then put it all into a package that provides great visuals to interact with. All times are in UTC. Every figure can be traced to a Nasa source.

JPL Horizons (independent check of Sun and Earth angles)

LOLA polar elevation grids (NASA PDS LOLA node)
Lunar landing and impact site coordinates (NASA NSSDCA)
